instructor.title: Meet your instructor
instructor.name: Carlos Cordova
bio: Hi, I'm Carlos. I'm a full-stack software engineer, and I didn't take the usual path to get here.

I earned my B.S. in Computer Engineering and my AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification while working full-time as a commercial truck driver and driver trainer. I studied data structures and algorithms between long shifts, so I know what it's like to learn this on top of a full day of work.

Training new drivers taught me to break hard skills into small, clear steps, and that's exactly how this course works. I built it to be the course I wish I'd had: visual, hands-on, and in both English and Spanish.

faq.a: Yes. The whole course is free during the beta.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: No. Lessons, animations and code all run in your browser.

faq.q: Is it in English or Spanish?
faq.a: Both. Pick your language on your first visit and switch any time from the top bar.
Every lesson lets you change and rerun the code, and each module's quiz explains every answer. An AI tutor that answers questions and gives hints is coming soon.

faq.q: Do I need to know data structures already?
faq.a: No. We start from zero with Big O and a method for solving problems. You only need basic JavaScript.

bigOGrowth.title: How Big O grows
bigOGrowth.constant: O(1): the line stays flat. The work doesn't grow with n.
bigOGrowth.log: O(log n): grows very slowly. Doubling n adds only one more step.
bigOGrowth.linear: O(n): a straight line. Twice the input means twice the work.
bigOGrowth.quadratic: O(n²): shoots up. At n = 1,000 it's already 1,000,000 operations.
bigOGrowth.summary: From best to worst: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n²).
bigOGrowth.nLogN: O(n log n): a bit steeper than O(n), and far below O(n²). Good sorting algorithms land here.
bigOGrowth.sortTitle: Where sort fits: O(n log n)
bigOGrowth.sortSummary: sort is O(n log n): slower than one pass over the array, much faster than comparing every pair.

arrayReindex.title: Array operations and re-indexing
arrayReindex.start: Every guest in the array has an index, starting at 0.
arrayReindex.push: push('Eli') adds to the end. No other guest moves: O(1).
arrayReindex.pop: pop() removes from the end. No other guest moves: O(1).
arrayReindex.shift: shift() removes the first guest, so every other guest moves down one index: O(n).
arrayReindex.unshift: unshift('Ana') adds to the start, so every guest moves up one index: O(n).

binarySearch.title: Binary search: cut the list in half
binarySearch.start: Find '{{target}}' in a guest list of {{count}} names sorted A to Z.
binarySearch.goRight: The middle name is '{{middle}}', which comes before '{{target}}' in ABC order: throw away the left half.
binarySearch.goLeft: The middle name is '{{middle}}', which comes after '{{target}}' in ABC order: throw away the right half.
binarySearch.found: Found '{{target}}' after {{checks}} checks. log₂(8) = 3: that's O(log n).

stopwatchRace.title: Timing the same code on two computers
stopwatchRace.start: The same code welcomes {{n}} guests. Let's time it on a fast laptop and an old phone.
stopwatchRace.firstRun: The laptop is much faster… but both did exactly {{n}} steps.
stopwatchRace.secondRun: Run it again: different times! Other apps and the browser change every run. The steps are still {{n}}.
stopwatchRace.moreGuests: Now {{n}} guests. The times change again, but the steps simply doubled to {{n}}.
stopwatchRace.summary: Seconds depend on the machine. Steps depend only on the code and n. Big O counts steps.
stopwatchRace.tooFast: A tiny job (2 guests): both show 0.0 ms. Code this fast can't be measured, so the stopwatch can't tell which version is faster.

searchCases.title: Best, average and worst case
searchCases.start: isInvited reads the list from the start. How much work it does depends on where the name is.
searchCases.best: '{{name}}' is first: found in {{checks}} check. The best case is called Ω (omega).
searchCases.average: '{{name}}' is in the middle: {{checks}} checks. The average case is called Θ (theta).
searchCases.worst: '{{name}}' isn't on the list: all {{checks}} names checked. The worst case is called O: big O.
searchCases.summary: Big O always means the worst case: the code will never be slower than this.

linearBoxes.title: O(n): one step per guest
linearBoxes.chartLabel: Steps grow in a straight line with the number of guests
linearBoxes.eight: Double the guests (8) and the work doubles too: 8 steps.
linearBoxes.line: The dots form a straight line. Work that grows like this is O(n), linear time.

constantJump.title: O(1): jump straight to the box
constantJump.start: The guest list. Each box has an index.
constantJump.jump: guests[3] jumps straight to box 3. No need to look at boxes 0, 1 and 2.
constantJump.length: guests.length is also just one step: the array already knows its size.
constantJump.huge: With a million guests, guests[500000] still jumps straight there: 1 step.
constantJump.summary: The work doesn't change with the size of the list. That's O(1), constant time: the best Big O.

sameShape.title: Drop the constants: same shape
sameShape.n: One loop over the guests: n steps. A straight line.
sameShape.twoN: Two loops in a row: 2n steps. Steeper, but still a straight line.
sameShape.threeN: 3n: steeper again, and still a straight line.
sameShape.nSquared: n² is different: it bends upward and leaves the others behind.
sameShape.summary: n, 2n and 3n have the same shape, so they are all O(n). We drop the constant.

nestedGrid.title: O(n²): every guest greets every guest
nestedGrid.start: Each row is a guest (i). For every row, the inner loop goes through every column (j).
nestedGrid.row: {{guest}}'s row is done: the inner loop ran {{n}} times. Grey cells are a guest meeting themselves (skipped).
nestedGrid.double: Double the guests to {{n}}: {{n}} × {{n}} = {{total}} steps. Twice the guests, 4 times the work!
nestedGrid.summary: A loop inside a loop over the same list is O(n²), quadratic time.

dominantTerm.title: Drop the non-dominant terms
dominantTerm.share: The n part is {{share}}% of the work.
dominantTerm.size: n = {{n}}: n² is {{squared}} and n adds only {{n}} more. The n part is {{share}}% of {{total}}.
dominantTerm.summary: As n grows, n² does almost all the work. So O(n² + n) is written O(n²).

twoInputs.title: Two inputs: guests (a) and helpers (b)
twoInputs.start: The party has 4 guests (a) and 2 helpers (b): two different lists.
twoInputs.guests: First loop: welcome every guest. That's a steps.
twoInputs.helpers: Then a second loop over the helpers: b more steps. In total: O(a + b).
twoInputs.grid: Now every guest thanks every helper: a loop over helpers inside a loop over guests. That's a × b steps: O(a · b).
twoInputs.summary: Don't call both sizes n: there could be 4 guests and 1,000 helpers. Use one letter per input.

memoryBoxes.title: Space: how much memory grows?
memoryBoxes.counter: Counting {{n}} guests only needs one box: the counter.
memoryBoxes.counterBig: With {{n}} guests it's still one box. O(1) space.
memoryBoxes.tags: Making a name tag for each of {{n}} guests needs a new box per guest.
memoryBoxes.tagsBig: {{n}} guests → {{n}} name tags. The memory grows with n: O(n) space.
memoryBoxes.summary: Space complexity counts the extra memory the code creates as the input grows.

halvingCount.title: Logarithms count halvings
halvingCount.start: 16 boxes. How many times can we cut them in half until 1 is left?
halvingCount.one: Only 1 left after {{halvings}} halvings. So log₂(16) = 4.
halvingCount.big: 1,024 boxes need only 10 halvings, and a million need about 20. That's why O(log n) is so fast.

isInvited.title: isInvited: stop as soon as you find the name
isInvited.start: Is '{{name}}' on the list of {{count}} guests? Start at i = 0.
isInvited.noMatch: Is guests[{{i}}] ('{{guest}}') equal to '{{name}}'? No → keep going.
isInvited.match: guests[{{i}}] is '{{guest}}'. Found it! Return true after {{ops}} checks.
isInvited.notFound: The loop ended: '{{name}}' isn't on the list. Return false after {{ops}} checks.

isInvitedAll.title: isInvitedAll: always read the whole list
isInvitedAll.start: Is '{{name}}' on the list of {{count}} guests? found starts as false.
isInvitedAll.match: guests[{{i}}] is '{{name}}': found = true… but the loop doesn't stop!
isInvitedAll.keepReading: '{{guest}}': we already found the name, but we keep reading anyway.
isInvitedAll.end: Return {{found}} after {{ops}} checks: every guest, every time.

countShortNames.title: Counting operations
countShortNames.loopCheck: Is i ({{i}}) < {{n}}? Yes, so the loop runs again: one operation.
countShortNames.isShort: '{{guest}}' has {{length}} letters, 3 or fewer: one operation for the check…
countShortNames.isLong: '{{guest}}' has {{length}} letters, more than 3: one operation for the check.
countShortNames.addOne: …and one for count = count + 1 (now {{count}}). Then i++ is one more.
countShortNames.fastForward: With {{n}} guests we skip to the end. Each guest costs 3 or 4 operations.
countShortNames.end: Done: {{ops}} operations for {{n}} guests. Try the other sizes: the total grows with n.

welcomeAll.title: welcomeAll: one message per guest
welcomeAll.start: Welcome {{n}} guests, one at a time.
welcomeAll.end: {{n}} guests → {{n}} messages. The work grows with n: O(n).

welcomeAndGoodbye.title: Two loops in a row
welcomeAndGoodbye.start: First welcome every guest, then say goodbye to every guest.
welcomeAndGoodbye.secondLoop: The first loop is done ({{n}} messages). Now the second loop starts.
welcomeAndGoodbye.end: {{n}} + {{n}} = {{total}} messages: 2n. Drop the constant: it's still O(n).

greetEveryone.title: greetEveryone: a loop inside a loop
greetEveryone.start: For each guest i, the inner loop goes through every guest j.
greetEveryone.self: i and j are both {{a}}: you don't greet yourself, but the inner loop still took a step.

partySummary.title: Rules of thumb: the cost of each line
partySummary.index: guests[0]: reading by index is one step. O(1).
partySummary.math: guests.length + 2: math on numbers is O(1), however big the numbers are.
partySummary.assign: let longNames = 0: giving a variable a value is O(1).
partySummary.inside: Inside the loop: one check and maybe one addition. O(1) each time…
partySummary.loop: …but the loop runs n times. Cost of a loop = times it runs × work inside = n × O(1) = O(n).
partySummary.total: Add it up: O(1) + O(1) + O(1) + O(n) + O(1). Drop the small terms: O(n).

countGuests.title: Counting every operation
countGuests.init: let count = 0: giving a variable a value is 1 operation.
countGuests.startLoop: let i = 0: 1 more operation. It runs only once, when the loop starts.
countGuests.compare: Is i ({{i}}) < {{n}}? A comparison: 1 operation. Yes, so the loop runs.
countGuests.add: count = count + 1: an addition and an assignment, 2 operations. count is now {{count}}.
countGuests.next: i++ is short for i = i + 1: 2 more operations. Back to the comparison.
countGuests.fastForward: With {{n}} guests we jump to the end. Every guest costs the same 5 operations.
countGuests.end: {{ops}} operations to count {{n}} guests: 5 per guest plus 3, or 5n + 3. guests.length gives the same answer ({{count}}) in 1 step.

giveGifts.title: A loop with a limit
giveGifts.start: {{n}} guests are on the list, but only the first 5 get a gift.
giveGifts.limit: i is {{i}}, so i < 5 is false: the loop stops, even though {{left}} guests are left.
giveGifts.noMoreGuests: No more guests: the loop ends before reaching the limit.
giveGifts.end: {{gifts}} gifts for {{n}} guests. Pick 20 guests: still 5. The loop never runs more than 5 times, so it's O(1).

sumLoop.title: sumUpTo: add the numbers one by one
sumLoop.init: let total = 0: 1 operation. It happens once, whatever n is.
sumLoop.startLoop: let i = 1: 1 more operation, also only once.
sumLoop.compare: Is i ({{i}}) <= n ({{n}})? A comparison: 1 operation. Yes, so the loop runs.
sumLoop.add: total = total + {{i}}: an addition and an assignment, 2 operations. total is now {{total}}. Then i++ adds 2 more.
sumLoop.fastForward: With n = {{n}} we skip to the end: every number costs the same 5 operations.
sumLoop.end: The sum of 1 to {{n}} is {{total}}, after {{ops}} operations: 5n + 2. The bigger n is, the more work.

sumFormula.title: sumUpToFormula: one formula, no loop
sumFormula.start: The same question for n = {{n}}, answered with a formula instead of a loop.
sumFormula.end: The sum of 1 to {{n}} is {{value}}, in 3 operations. Try n = 1,000,000: still 3.

printNumbers.title: printNumbers: n in, n lines out
printNumbers.start: Give the function n = {{n}}. The loop goes from i = 0 while i < {{n}}.
printNumbers.end: We passed in {{n}} and it ran {{n}} times: {{n}} lines. That's O(n).

printPairs.title: printPairs: a loop inside a loop
printPairs.start: For every i, the inner loop goes through every j.

doubleArray.title: doubleArray: a new array that grows
doubleArray.start: doubled starts as an empty array. It's new memory the function creates.
doubleArray.end: {{n}} numbers in, {{n}} new boxes of memory. The extra memory grows with n: O(n) space.

hasAnswer.title: hasAnswer: look for a value, answer by answer
hasAnswer.start: Did anyone answer '{{answer}}'? Object.keys gives us the {{count}} names to loop over.
hasAnswer.match: {{name}} answered '{{answer}}'. Found it! Return true after {{ops}} checks.
hasAnswer.notFound: The loop ended: nobody answered '{{answer}}'. Return false after {{ops}} checks.

charCount.title: charCount, the simple version, character by character
charCount.start: charCount('{{text}}'): an empty object to fill and {{count}} characters to read.
charCount.firstTime: {{char}} isn't a key yet: result[{{char}}] is undefined, and undefined > 0 is false. Set it to 1.
charCount.again: {{char}} is already a key, so add 1. It's at {{count}} now.
charCount.done: All {{ops}} characters read, in one pass: O(n). The object has {{keys}} keys.

timingChart.title: Timing both versions as n grows
timingChart.start: We time sumUpTo for bigger and bigger n, from 200 million to 1 billion, and put each time on a chart.
timingChart.firstPoint: With n = 200 million, the loop takes about a quarter of a second.
timingChart.loopLine: Each time n grows by 200 million, the time grows by about the same amount. The points line up: a straight line.
timingChart.formula: The formula takes almost no time, whatever n is: a flat line along the bottom.
timingChart.noise: These are example times. Run it on your computer and they'll be a little different, and tiny inputs jump around. What stays the same is the shape.
timingChart.summary: The loop's time grows in a line with n (O(n)); the formula's stays flat (O(1)). Big O names these shapes.

arraySplice.title: Adding and removing in the middle
arraySplice.start: Five guests, each with an index.
arraySplice.insert: splice(1, 0, 'Zoe') puts Zoe at index 1. Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli all move up one index.
arraySplice.remove: splice(2, 1) removes Ben. Cleo, Dev and Eli all move down one index.
arraySplice.notHalf: In the middle, about half the items move, but it's still O(n): Big O is the worst case (inserting at index 0 moves them all), and ½n drops its constant anyway.

arrayVsObject.title: Two free data structures: an array and an object
arrayVsObject.start: The same party stored two ways. The array keeps the guests in order; the object labels each answer with the guest's name.
arrayVsObject.access: Reading with an index or a key jumps straight to one box. Both are O(1).
arrayVsObject.addEnd: Adding to the end of the array, or adding a new key to the object, touches one box. Both are O(1).
arrayVsObject.addStart: Adding to the start is different. The array has to re-index every guest: O(n). The object has no start, so it still touches one box.
arrayVsObject.search: Searching for something that isn't there means checking every box, in both: O(n).
arrayVsObject.summary: Arrays give you order. Objects give you fast keys but no order. Every data structure is a trade-off like this one.

access.title: Reading a key: one jump
access.start: The answers object: 5 guests, 5 keys. No indexes, and no first or last key.
access.read: rsvps['Dev'] goes straight to Dev's card. It doesn't look at Ana, Ben or Cleo first: 1 box.
access.dot: rsvps.Eli is the same lookup written with a dot. Eli was added last, but that doesn't make it slower.
access.missing: 'Zoe' isn't a key. JavaScript goes straight to where Zoe's card would be, finds nothing and returns undefined: still 1 step.
access.huge: A party of a million guests: rsvps['Zoe'] still jumps straight to Zoe. 1 box, whatever the size.
access.summary: Reading a key is O(1), constant time, just like reading an array by its index.

write.title: Adding, changing and deleting keys
write.add: rsvps['Fay'] = 'yes' adds a new key. No other card moves or changes: O(1).
write.update: Ben changed his mind. Updating is a lookup plus a new value: O(1).
write.remove: delete rsvps['Cleo'] removes one key. Nobody has an index, so nobody is re-indexed: O(1).
write.summary: Adding, changing and deleting each touched one card. Compare that with shift and unshift on an array.

hasKey.title: Is this key there? Is this value there?
hasKey.start: Two questions: is a guest on the list (a key), and did anyone answer 'late' (a value)?
hasKey.has: hasOwnProperty('Dev') jumps to where Dev's key would be. It's there: true. 1 box, O(1).
hasKey.hasNot: hasOwnProperty('Zoe') jumps to where Zoe's key would be. Nothing's there: false. Still 1 step.
hasKey.value: Values have no shortcut. To know if anyone said 'late', every answer has to be read: O(n).
hasKey.summary: Checking for a key is O(1). Searching for a value is O(n).

objectToArray.title: Object.keys builds a new array
objectToArray.start: Object.keys(rsvps) starts with an empty array.
objectToArray.firstKey: It visits the first key, '{{key}}', and copies it into the new array: 1 step.
objectToArray.nextKey: Next key: '{{key}}'. That's {{count}} steps so far.
objectToArray.keysDone: Every key was visited once: {{n}} keys, {{n}} steps and {{n}} new boxes of memory.
objectToArray.values: Object.values takes the same walk, copying the answers instead of the names.
objectToArray.entries: Object.entries copies both, as [key, value] pairs. A bit more work per key, but still one visit per key.
objectToArray.summary: Double the keys and you double the work and the memory: O(n) time and O(n) space.

copies.title: concat, slice and splice: how many boxes?
copies.start: Six guests. Each method below copies or moves some of them. Count the boxes it touches.
copies.concat: concat copies every item of both arrays into a new one: 6 + 3 = 9 boxes. That's O(n + m), which we simply call O(n).
copies.slice: slice(1, 4) copies the items from index 1 up to (but not including) index 4: 3 boxes. The cost is the size of the copy.
copies.sliceAll: slice() with no arguments copies the whole array: all 6 boxes. In the worst case, O(n).
copies.spliceMiddle: splice(2, 0, 'Zoe') inserts Zoe at index 2. Every guest after her moves up one index: 5 boxes.
copies.spliceStart: At index 0, splice moves everyone: 7 boxes. Big O takes this worst case: O(n).
copies.summary: All three grow with the size of the array: O(n).

loops.title: forEach, map, filter and reduce: hidden loops
loops.start: Five guests. Each of these methods runs your function once for every guest.
loops.forEach: forEach visits every guest once to print the name: 5 boxes. It returns nothing.
loops.map: map visits every guest and builds a new array of the same length: 5 visits, 5 new boxes.
loops.filter: filter visits every guest and keeps the ones that pass the test (3-letter names): 5 visits, 4 kept.
loops.reduce: reduce visits every guest and combines them into one value, the total length of their names: {{value}}.
loops.summary: One line each, but each one is a loop over the whole array: O(n).

map.title: The 5 steps for any problem
map.start: A problem you've never seen, and no idea where to start. Here's a plan you can follow every time.
map.understand: Step 1: understand the problem. Before any code, make sure you know what goes in, what comes out and what's missing.
map.examples: Step 2: explore examples. Write a few inputs with the output you expect, from easy ones to strange ones.
map.breakDown: Step 3: break it down. Write the steps as short comments, so you have a direction.
map.solve: Step 4: solve it, or solve a simpler version first and add the hard part back later.
map.lookBack: Step 5: look back and refactor. It works, so now make it clearer, faster, or both.
map.summary: Understand, explore, break it down, solve, look back. You'll use these 5 steps for the rest of the course.

understand.title: Step 1: understand the problem
understand.start: Before writing code, ask five questions: out loud in an interview, or to yourself at home.
items: Can I explain it back in my own words?
Is that enough to get the answer?
notes: Explaining it back in your own words proves you understood it, and catches mistakes before they become code.
Inputs: what goes in, what type it is, how big it can get and how many there are.
Outputs: what comes back, and in what shape: a number, a string, an object?
Sometimes something is missing, like a second number. You may only notice later, and that's fine.
Good names now (add, num1, num2, sum) make every next step easier to talk about.
understand.summary: Five questions, a minute or two. They're the cheapest way to avoid solving the wrong problem.

examples.title: Step 2: explore examples
examples.start: Examples turn a problem written in words into inputs and outputs you can check.
items: Move on to more complex examples
notes: Simple examples first: the easiest inputs, with outputs you're sure about.
Then harder ones: spaces, capital letters, digits. Each one tends to raise a question.
Empty inputs, like '' or []: what should come back?
Invalid inputs, like a number where a string should be: return something, or stop with an error?
examples.summary: Write your examples down. When your code is done, they're the first tests you run.

breakDown.title: Step 3: break it down
breakDown.start: Before the real code, write the steps you'll take, in plain words.
items: Write the main steps as comments
Think about the logic before the syntax
Spot the parts you don't know yet
notes: Not every line, and not real code: just the main steps, as short comments.
Deciding what to do first means you don't fight the syntax and the logic at the same time.
Writing the plan shows the steps you're unsure about, so you can ask about them early.
breakDown.summary: A plan written down is something you can show, check and come back to, even if time runs out.

solve.title: Step 4: solve or simplify
solve.start: Can you solve all of it? Great. If not, solve a simpler problem first.
notes: Find the one part that's tripping you up, like checking whether a character is a letter.
Ignore it for a moment. Simplify the problem, don't change it.
Write a working solution for everything else. Now you have real code to show and to run.
Bring the hard part back. Often the simple version has shown you how to do it.
solve.summary: Some progress beats none, and the simpler problem is often the road into the harder one.

lookBack.title: Step 5: look back and refactor
lookBack.start: It works. Before you stop, ask these questions about your solution.
items: Is there another way to get there?
Can it be faster, or use less memory?
How did other people solve it?
notes: Check the result: run your examples from step 2 again.
There's rarely only one solution. Now that you've solved it once, a second way may be easy to see.
Is it easy to read? Would a teammate understand it on a whiteboard?
Does it look like a problem you've solved before, or one you'll meet later?
Performance: its Big O in time and space. Nested loops are the first thing to look at.
Style: clear names, let and const, the conventions of the language and your team.
Other people's solutions, even in another language, are a great way to learn new tricks.
lookBack.summary: Looking back is where you learn the most. Every problem you review makes the next one easier.

exampleLadder.title: Examples for charCount, from easy to strange
exampleLadder.start: The problem: count how many times each character appears in a string. Let's write examples before any code.
exampleLadder.row0: 'aaa' is easy: one character, three times. The output is an object: { a: 3 }.
exampleLadder.row1: 'banana' is still easy, and shows the shape of the answer: one key per character, with its count.
exampleLadder.row2: 'Hi Ana!' raises questions. Do we count the space? The '!'? Are 'H' and 'h' the same letter?
exampleLadder.row3: 'Party at 8!' adds a digit. Should '8' be counted?
exampleLadder.row4: An empty string: return an empty object, or something else?
exampleLadder.row5: A number instead of a string: return something, or stop with an error?
exampleLadder.decided: Our answers: count letters and digits only, in lowercase, and accept only strings. Each answer came from an example.
exampleLadder.onlyStrings: Not a string: we only accept strings

stepsToCode.title: From a plan in comments to code
stepsToCode.start: First, the plan: six comments and no code. This is what you'd write before anything else.

comments.loop: loop over the string, one character at a time
comments.addOne: a letter or digit that's already a key: add 1
comments.setOne: a letter or digit that's not a key yet: set it to 1

stepsToCode.makeObject: The easy part first: an empty object, result, to fill and return.
stepsToCode.loop: The loop over the string. We lowercase each character as we read it, so 'H' and 'h' count together.
stepsToCode.addOne: A character that's already a key gets 1 more. isAlphaNumeric doesn't exist yet: we gave the step a name and kept going.
stepsToCode.setOne: A new letter or digit starts at 1.
stepsToCode.skip: Spaces and punctuation: nothing to do, so all that's left is to close the if and the loop.
stepsToCode.returnIt: Return the object. Every comment now has its code.
stepsToCode.summary: The comments were the plan, and the plan became the code. Only isAlphaNumeric is left to write.

solutionLayers.title: Solve a simpler problem, then add the hard parts back
solutionLayers.simple: Layer 1: the simple charCount. It ignores case and doesn't check what kind of character it reads.
solutionLayers.simpleOutput: On 'Hi Ana!' it runs, but 'H' and 'A' are counted apart from 'h' and 'a', and the space and '!' are counted too.
solutionLayers.lowercase: Layer 2: one change. Each character is lowercased as we read it.
solutionLayers.lowercaseOutput: Now 'a' has 2. Only the space and '!' are still wrong.
solutionLayers.check: Layer 3: the hard part comes back. Only letters and digits get counted.
solutionLayers.checkOutput: The right answer. Nothing from layer 1 was thrown away: each layer only added code.

charCodeRanges.title: Character codes: is it a letter or a digit?
charCodeRanges.start: Every character has a number. The digits, the capital letters and the lowercase letters each fill one block of numbers.
charCodeRanges.inside: {{char}} has code {{code}}. It's inside a green block: a letter or a digit.
charCodeRanges.outside: {{char}} has code {{code}}. It's outside every green block: not a letter or a digit.
charCodeRanges.summary: Three range checks answer the question, with no regular expression. Watch the edges: '[' is 91, one past 'Z', and '`' is 96, one before 'a'.

instances.title: One class, many cookies
instances.start: class Cookie is the cookie cutter: a shape you can use again and again. On its own, it isn't a cookie yet.
instances.first: new Cookie('chocolate') stamps out the first cookie, an instance named cookieOne, with its own flavor.
instances.second: The same cutter makes a second instance, cookieTwo. Same shape, different flavor.
instances.summary: One class, two instances. Each cookie keeps its own data, and you can stamp out as many as you need.

new.title: What new does, in four small steps
new.start: new Cookie('chocolate') looks like one action, but JavaScript does four things.
new.empty: 1. It makes a brand-new, empty object.
new.this: 2. It points this at that object, so the constructor knows which cookie it's building.
new.run: 3. It runs the constructor. this.flavor = 'chocolate' writes the flavor onto the new object.
new.returned: 4. It returns the finished object, and cookieOne now points to it.

methods.title: Getters and setters: each cookie answers for itself
methods.start: Two instances of the same class: cookieOne is chocolate and cookieTwo is vanilla.
methods.getOne: cookieOne.getFlavor() runs with this pointing at cookieOne, so it returns 'chocolate'.
methods.getTwo: Same method, called on cookieTwo: this is cookieTwo now, so it returns 'vanilla'.
methods.set: cookieOne.setFlavor('oatmeal') changes only cookieOne. cookieTwo isn't touched.
methods.getAgain: Reading it again shows the change: cookieOne.getFlavor() is now 'oatmeal'.
methods.summary: Getters read an instance's data and setters change it. Both work on this: whichever cookie you called them on.

listClassPreview.title: A preview: the LinkedList class at work
listClassPreview.create: new LinkedList('Ana') creates a list with one guest. The constructor sets everything up.
listClassPreview.push: push('Ben') adds a guest at the end.
listClassPreview.unshift: unshift('Zoe') adds a guest at the start.
listClassPreview.insert: insert(1, 'Cleo') puts a guest at index 1, between Zoe and Ana.
listClassPreview.remove: remove(1) takes out the guest at index 1: Cleo leaves.
listClassPreview.pop: pop() removes the last guest, Ben.
listClassPreview.shift: shift() removes the first guest, Zoe.
listClassPreview.summary: Each method did one specific job on the list. In the Linked Lists module you'll write every one of them yourself.

valueCopy.title: Copying a number copies the value
valueCopy.copy: let seats = guestCount copies the 5 into seats. Now there are two separate 5s.
valueCopy.change: guestCount = 8 changes only guestCount. seats still holds its own 5.
valueCopy.summary: seats is still 5. Numbers, strings and booleans are copied, so changing one variable never changes the other.

referenceCopy.title: Copying an object copies the arrow
referenceCopy.start: card doesn't hold the object itself: it holds an arrow to object A, { value: 'Ana' }.
referenceCopy.copy: let sameCard = card copies the arrow, not the object. Both variables now point to the same object A.
referenceCopy.change: card.value = 'Ben' follows card's arrow and changes object A.
referenceCopy.read: sameCard follows its arrow to the same object, so sameCard.value is 'Ben' too.
referenceCopy.summary: card === sameCard is true: they're the same object. There's still only one object A.

pointerMove.title: Moving pointers, and garbage collection
pointerMove.start: first points to object A, { value: 'Ana' }.
pointerMove.second: let second = first: second points to object A too.
pointerMove.third: let third = { value: 'Cleo' } makes a new object B, and third points to it.
pointerMove.moveSecond: second = third moves second's arrow to object B. Object A still has first.
pointerMove.moveFirst: first = third moves the last arrow away from A. Nothing points to object A any more, so nothing can reach it.
pointerMove.collected: JavaScript's garbage collector finds objects nothing points to and frees their memory. Object A is gone.
